textTitles: White gold: how salt shaped trade
Is the lecture past its best?

paragraphs.text: For most of history, a writer who published a book had no legal control over what happened to it next. Anyone with access to a copy and a means of reproducing it could make and sell further copies, and authors earned money, if they earned any at all, from patrons, from a single payment by a publisher or from the prestige that authorship brought. Some were paid nothing and expected nothing, since writing was regarded as a gentleman’s pastime rather than a trade. The idea that a text belongs to its author in the way that a house belongs to its owner, and that copying it without permission is a kind of theft, is surprisingly recent. It developed over roughly three centuries, and it grew less from concern for writers than from disputes between the businesses that printed and sold their work.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The printing press, which spread across Europe in the second half of the fifteenth century, made copying fast and cheap for the first time. Rulers quickly saw both the danger and the opportunity. Books could spread ideas that governments wished to suppress, and so many states began to grant printers exclusive rights to publish particular titles in exchange for submitting them for approval. These privileges, as they were called, protected the printer’s investment by keeping rivals out of the market. They were a favour from the ruler rather than a right, however, and they belonged to the business that held them, not to the person who had written the book. A rival who printed the same book without a privilege could have his copies seized.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: In England, the system took the form of a monopoly held by a guild of printers and booksellers, whose members registered titles and could prevent anyone else from printing them. When the government allowed the law behind this monopoly to lapse at the end of the seventeenth century, the guild lobbied hard for new protection. The statute that followed in 1710 is often described as the first copyright law. Its title presented it as a measure for the encouragement of learning, and it gave the right to print a book, for a limited period, to its author or to whoever the author sold that right to. For the first time, the law recognised the writer as the starting point of ownership.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The limit on the period of protection proved to be the most contested part of the new law. The statute granted fourteen years, renewable once if the author was still alive, after which anyone could print the work. London booksellers, who had grown used to treating their titles as permanent property, argued that authors possessed a natural right in their writing that no statute could end, and for several decades they continued to act as though their rights were unlimited. The question was finally settled by the highest court in 1774, which ruled against them. The judges held that whatever rights an author might once have had were now defined by the statute alone. Once the term had expired, a book belonged to everyone, and cheap editions of older literature soon appeared in large numbers.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Elsewhere, ideas about authorship developed along different lines. In France, the laws passed after the revolution of 1789 described an author’s work as the most sacred and personal of all forms of property, and later legal writers added the notion of moral rights: the author’s right to be named as the creator of a work and to object to changes that damage it, even after the economic rights have been sold. This tradition places more weight on the bond between creator and creation, while the English tradition treats copyright mainly as a commercial arrangement designed to encourage the production of new work. The difference still matters today, for example when a film company wishes to alter a novel it has bought.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Neither tradition could protect authors across borders. Throughout the nineteenth century, popular books were reprinted without payment in countries where their authors had no rights, and some of the most widely read novelists of the age complained bitterly that they earned nothing from the huge sales of pirated editions abroad. Publishers in those countries argued that cheap reprints spread education and that foreign authors had done nothing to deserve payment there. An international agreement signed in Bern in 1886 required member countries to give foreign authors the same protection as their own, and it gradually became the basis of copyright law in most of the world. Some large book markets, however, joined only many decades later.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Since then the period of protection has been extended repeatedly. In much of the world it now lasts for the author’s lifetime and seventy years after, so that a novel written by a young author today may not enter the public domain until the end of the next century. Supporters of long terms argue that they allow authors to provide for their families and give publishers a reason to invest in keeping books in print. Critics reply that the vast majority of books stop earning money within a few years of publication, and that long terms mainly prevent libraries, teachers and other writers from using works whose owners can no longer even be traced.
paragraphs.label: G

texts.title: White gold: how salt shaped trade

paragraphs.text: It is easy to forget how valuable salt once was. Today it is so cheap that it is spread on icy roads by the tonne, but for most of history it was one of the most traded goods in the world. It was even used as a form of money in some places, and Roman soldiers were sometimes said to have been paid in it, a story that is probably untrue but shows how highly it was valued. People need a certain amount of salt to stay healthy, and farming communities, whose diet of grain contained little of it, had to obtain it from elsewhere. Above all, salt was the only reliable way of preserving meat and fish before refrigeration, and a society that could not preserve food through the winter or transport it over long distances was limited in what it could achieve.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Salt can be obtained in three main ways, and each shaped the places where it was produced. Along warm coasts, seawater was let into shallow pans and left for the sun and wind to evaporate, a method that needed flat land, reliable sunshine and a great deal of patience. Inland, springs of salty water could be boiled over fires until the salt crystallised, which consumed enormous quantities of wood; some producing regions stripped their surrounding forests bare. The third source was rock salt, the remains of ancient seas buried underground, which could be mined in solid blocks, though only a few places had deposits close enough to the surface to reach. Each method also produced salt of a slightly different quality, and buyers were often willing to pay more for particular kinds.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Because good sources were unevenly distributed, salt had to travel, and the routes it followed were among the oldest trade roads in Europe, Africa and Asia. Across the Sahara, caravans carried slabs of rock salt south from desert mines to the markets of West Africa, where it was exchanged, according to later accounts, for gold, sometimes weight for weight. The journey could take weeks, and the slabs were often cut to a standard size so that they could be counted rather than weighed. In central Europe, towns whose names still contain old words for salt grew rich from springs or mines and from the tolls charged on the roads that led away from them. Several of these towns built impressive bridges, halls and churches with the profits, and many of those buildings survive.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Governments were quick to see salt as a source of revenue. Because everyone needed it and there was no substitute, a tax on salt was difficult to avoid and brought in a steady income. It could also be collected at a small number of production sites rather than from millions of individual buyers. In ancient China, the state took control of salt production and sale in order to pay for its armies, and a famous debate at the imperial court in the first century BC set officials who defended the monopoly against scholars who argued that it burdened ordinary people. Similar taxes existed across Europe for centuries, and in France the salt tax became so hated that its abolition was among the early demands of the revolution.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The burden of such taxes fell most heavily on the poor, who spent a far larger share of their income on salt than the rich did. Smuggling was common wherever the tax was high, and governments employed large numbers of officials to prevent it. In some regions households were required to buy a fixed minimum quantity of taxed salt each year, whether they needed it or not. Historians have used the records of these compulsory purchases to estimate population and household size in periods for which no other figures survive. Complaints about the tax appear again and again in petitions from rural areas, where salt was needed in large quantities to preserve meat for the winter.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The importance of salt declined in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. New methods of drilling and pumping made underground deposits far easier to exploit, railways reduced the cost of moving heavy goods, and canning and later refrigeration offered other ways to preserve food. Salt that had once been carried hundreds of kilometres by animals could now be delivered by train in a matter of days. As prices fell, salt taxes lost much of their value to governments, and most were abolished or reduced to a minor charge. Salt, once worth fighting over, became one of the cheapest things in the kitchen.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Yet the history of salt has not entirely disappeared. The majority of salt produced today is not eaten at all but used by the chemical industry, where it is a raw material for making substances such as chlorine and soda. Traditional coastal salt works have in some places been revived, partly for the high prices that hand-harvested salt can command and partly because the shallow pans provide valuable habitats for birds. Some of the old inland salt towns, meanwhile, have turned their former industry into a tourist attraction, and the mines and boiling houses that once paid for their bridges now charge admission. Visitors can see how the work was done, though rarely how hard it was.
paragraphs.label: G

texts.title: Is the lecture past its best?

paragraphs.text: The lecture is one of the oldest teaching methods still in everyday use. In medieval universities, where books were rare and expensive, a lecturer read aloud from a text while students wrote it down, and the word itself comes from the Latin for reading. Books have long since become cheap, and recorded lectures can now be watched at any time, yet the basic arrangement survives almost unchanged: one person speaking, often for an hour, to a room full of people who mostly listen. Few other institutions have kept a working method for so long. Critics have been predicting its end for decades. It is worth asking why it has lasted, and whether it deserves to. Both questions deserve a careful answer.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The case against the lecture rests largely on research into how students learn. The education researcher Maria Santos, who has reviewed hundreds of studies comparing traditional lectures with classes in which students solve problems and discuss ideas, reports that students in the more active classes perform better on examinations and are considerably less likely to fail. The effect was largest for students who had struggled at school. Her conclusion is that listening, however attentive, is a poor way to acquire the ability to use knowledge, as opposed to merely recognising it. Santos also notes that attention in a lecture tends to fall sharply after the first quarter of an hour. Her review includes studies from many subjects, from physics to history, and the pattern is similar in all of them.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: I find this evidence hard to dismiss, but I think it is sometimes stretched further than it can go. Many of the studies compare a poor lecture with a well-designed active class, and a well-prepared lecturer who pauses to ask questions is not the same as one who reads from slides. The psychologist James Whitfield points out that students often rate active classes less highly than lectures, even when they learn more in them, because active learning feels harder; the sense of effort is mistaken for a sign of failure. This finding cuts both ways. It suggests that students’ preferences are a poor guide to what helps them, but also that simply asking students whether a course works is unlikely to reveal it. Whitfield’s own students, he admits, complained loudly when he first abandoned his lectures.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Supporters of the lecture make an argument from economics. A single lecturer can teach several hundred students at once, while discussion-based teaching requires small groups and therefore many more staff. The economist Oliver Grant has calculated that replacing lectures entirely with small-group teaching would roughly triple the cost of teaching at a typical university, a sum that few institutions could find without raising fees or cutting other services. He accepts that active methods are more effective, but argues that the relevant question is not which method is best in principle but which is best for a given amount of money. His figures assume that class sizes would remain as they are, which may not be realistic.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: There is also an argument that the lecture does something that other methods cannot. A good lecturer does not simply transmit information, which students could find in a book; he or she shows how an expert thinks about a problem, which questions matter and how evidence is weighed. The historian Clara Nkemelu, who has studied lecturing traditions in several countries, argues that the best lectures are performances of reasoning, and that students who watch an expert work through an argument in real time learn habits of mind that are rarely taught explicitly anywhere else. Such teaching, she adds, depends heavily on the skill of the individual lecturer, and not every lecturer possesses it.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The spread of recorded lectures has complicated the debate. Many universities now record lectures as a matter of course, and attendance has fallen at a number of them, since students can watch at home, pause and replay difficult passages, or watch at double speed before an examination. Others still attend, some because they value the routine and the company of other students. Some lecturers regard this as a threat; others have used it as an opportunity, recording short explanations in advance and using the scheduled time for discussion and problem-solving instead. This approach, sometimes called flipped teaching, keeps much of what is valuable in the lecture while removing the part that could be done equally well by a recording.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: My own view is that the question is badly framed. The lecture as a single hour of uninterrupted talk to a silent audience is hard to defend, and the evidence against it is strong; few lecturers would now defend it in that form. But the lecture as a way for an expert to explain, demonstrate and provoke is worth keeping, and it can be combined with activity rather than replaced by it. What should disappear is not the lecturer but the silence. A lecture in which students are asked to think, rather than merely to write things down, is not the relic of a medieval university but one of the more effective tools that a modern one has. Universities that recognise this will keep their lecture halls but change what happens inside them.
paragraphs.label: G
